How we decide

For each everyday thing, the lexicon recommends one Latin word and shows the others. These are the rules behind those choices. Our rulings on particular words and rules are on a page of their own, each with its evidence, its date and who made it. Any of them can be reopened: if you think we got one wrong, tell us why.

The rulesNotesRulings (23)

The rules

  1. Classical first. A word that classical authors use in the sense we need comes first. A post-classical word fills a real gap and must be well attested; Christian Latin is the natural source for church life (benedīcere). A coinage comes last, and a coinage of our own is labelled as ours.
  2. Source order. For modern things we consult Traupman’s Conversational Latin, then the Morgan–Owens Neo-Latin lexicon, then Levi and Bini’s Il latino come lingua viva (1937), whose words we check in Lewis & Short because it cites no sources, then the Vatican’s Lexicon Recentis Latinitatis and other modern lexica. On Latinity, classical usage outranks them all, and Smith & Hall and Morgan–Owens outrank Traupman: the chimney is camīnus, not Traupman’s fūmārium.
  3. Show every form. Where the sources differ, every form appears, the recommended one first, each labelled with its period: classical, late, medieval, Renaissance, modern, or ours.
  4. Flag false friends. A modern form that meant something else in antiquity is listed with the reason it is not used.
  5. Label register. Words that are chiefly comic, poetic or colloquial say so.
  6. Vowel length. Macrons are part of the spelling, so every long vowel is marked. Our authorities, in order: Lewis & Short; Bennett for hidden quantities that Lewis & Short leaves unmarked; and de Vaan’s Etymological Dictionary of Latin wherever he discusses the vowel. A vowel we cannot settle stays unmarked, and the entry says so.
  7. Spelling. Consonantal i is written j (jam, ejus, conjungō). Search ignores the difference, and ignores macrons too.
  8. Examples. Every example sentence is marked either as a quotation, with its source, or as composed by us.
  9. Review. Every change is checked automatically for its format, its links and its spelling of j. Entries drafted with machine help stay marked as drafts until a person has reviewed them.

Notes

Wherever an entry departs from Lewis & Short or from one of its sources, a numbered note gives the reason and the evidence. A note that rests on one of our rulings links to it. The notes are there so that you can check our reasoning, and so that we can trace a mistake to the decision that caused it.

Rulings

A ruling is a recorded decision: a rule for many words, or a choice on one word where we depart from a dictionary or a source. All 23 are on the rulings page, with their evidence, history and the words that cite them.
